chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya and others, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Ali ibn al-Mughira, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'May I be sacrificed for you! Is benefit derived from anything of the dead animal (maytah)?' He said: 'No.' I said, 'It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by a dead sheep and said: 'What was upon the owners of this sheep? If they did not benefit from its flesh, they could have benefited from its skin?' He said: 'That sheep belonged to Sawda bint Zama'a, the wife of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), and it was a skinny sheep from which no benefit was derived from its flesh, so they left it until it died. So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'What was upon its owners? If they did not benefit from its flesh, they could have benefited from its skin' — if it had been slaughtered (thakka).
ai.seo_question: Can the skin of a dead animal be used for leather in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies the general Shia ruling that the carcass of a dead animal (maytah) is impure and unusable, while resolving an apparent contradiction with a specific prophetic incident involving the sheep of Sawdah bint Zam'ah. The Imam explains that the Prophet's permission to benefit from its skin was a specific exception due to the animal's emaciated state, establishing that the skin requires proper tanning (thakka) to become pure for use in prayer garments. This distinction is crucial in fiqh for determining the validity of clothing worn during Salāt.
